_comment: Gold set for cluster 17 (AI/ML Startup Compliance). Drafted by Claude on 11 Aug 2026 against a deliberately-constructed document (Talentyx) whose intended verdicts are known. Every 'nuanced' case is a genuine legal judgement call and is the priority for human/lawyer review. Verdicts here are a DRAFT to be corrected, not ground truth yet.

profile.talentyx: AI CV-screening SaaS, 55 staff, Berlin. Fine-tunes an open-weights model and sells the result under its own mark = provider of a high-risk (Annex III employment) AI system. Constructed to span the full verdict range and to include genuine compliance, not only gaps.

cases.evidence_in_document: we treat Talentyx Screen as a high-risk AI system. We have documented this classification and the reasons for it.
cases.rationale: Candidate screening for employment is Annex III point 4. They correctly classify and document it. The obligation is to make and document the determination, which they have done.

cases.evidence_in_document: does not use subliminal or manipulative techniques, does not perform social scoring, does not scrape facial images, and does not infer emotions.
cases.rationale: None of the eight Article 5 practices are present, and the terms prohibit misuse. Nothing to remediate.

cases.evidence_in_document: We do not generate images, audio or video of any kind.
cases.rationale: The two new prohibitions concern generation of intimate imagery and CSAM. A text-ranking product that generates no such media cannot engage them.

cases.evidence_in_document: All engineering and customer-success staff completed a four-hour internal training on the EU AI Act ... New joiners complete it during onboarding, and we repeat it annually.
cases.rationale: A documented, recurring literacy programme covering the relevant staff meets the Article 4 measure-taking obligation.

cases.evidence_in_document: Every candidate-facing page carries a persistent banner reading 'Screening assisted by AI', and recruiters see a tooltip explaining that the scores are generated by a model.
cases.rationale: People interacting with the system are told it is AI. That is the Article 50(1) interaction-disclosure duty; no synthetic media duty arises.

cases.evidence_in_document: We have not separately analysed whether our fine-tuning of the base model changes our legal role from deployer to provider, and our terms currently describe us as a 'technology supplier'.
cases.rationale: Fine-tuning a model and placing the result on the market under your own trade mark makes you the provider under Article 25(1). They have not recognised this, which is the substantive gap: every high-risk provider duty follows from it. REVIEW: is 'gap' right, or is this 'partial' because they at least treat the system as high-risk?

cases.evidence_in_document: We measure selection-rate differences across gender and age bands quarterly and retrain if the difference exceeds our internal threshold.
cases.rationale: Article 10 data-governance / bias examination is partly evidenced by the quarterly selection-rate testing. But there is no documented continuous risk-management system (Art 9) and no accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity declaration (Art 15). Partial rather than met. Note the duty only binds from 2 Dec 2027.

cases.evidence_in_document: We maintain an internal model card ... We keep a changelog of model versions. ... We have not drawn up the Annex IV technical documentation
cases.rationale: Logging (changelog) and human oversight are present, but the Annex IV technical documentation is explicitly absent. Partial. REVIEW: a model card is not Annex IV documentation, so an assessor might call this 'gap'.

cases.evidence_in_document: we have not carried out a conformity assessment, we have not affixed a CE marking
cases.rationale: No quality management system, no conformity assessment, no CE marking. ISO 27001 is an information-security standard, not the Article 17 QMS. Clear gap.

cases.evidence_in_document: we have not registered the product in any EU database.
cases.rationale: A high-risk Annex III provider must register itself and the system before placing it on the market. Not done.

cases.evidence_in_document: We build and sell 'Talentyx Screen' ... Recruiters review the ranked list and decide whom to interview.
cases.rationale: Talentyx is the provider; the deployer duties in Articles 26-27 bind its customers (the employers), not Talentyx. REVIEW: if Talentyx also runs the system on its own account for any customer, it could wear both hats.

cases.evidence_in_document: The product is sold under the Talentyx name ... Recruiters review the ranked list and decide whom to interview.
cases.rationale: The FRIA binds specific DEPLOYERS (public bodies, public-service providers, credit and insurance). Talentyx is the provider and is a private company, so Article 27 does not bind it. Its employer-customers may owe a FRIA. REVIEW: confirm none of Talentyx's own uses put it in a deployer role.

cases.evidence_in_document: We measure selection-rate differences ... quarterly ... Our incident response plan defines severity levels
cases.rationale: Monitoring activities exist (bias metrics, incident plan, changelog), but there is no documented post-market monitoring SYSTEM built on a post-market monitoring PLAN as Article 72 requires. Partial.

cases.evidence_in_document: We do not currently have a procedure for reporting serious incidents to a market surveillance authority.
cases.rationale: Article 73 requires reporting serious incidents to the market surveillance authority within 15 days (10 for a death, 2 for widespread infringement). They report to customers only. Gap.

cases.evidence_in_document: We fine-tune a third-party open-weights language model on our own annotated dataset ... 'Talentyx Screen', a SaaS product
cases.rationale: They place a specific-purpose SYSTEM on the market, not a general-purpose MODEL. Fine-tuning a base model for hiring does not make them a GPAI provider. Article 53 binds providers of GPAI models placed on the market as models. REVIEW: this is the classic provider-role trap; confirm they never distribute the fine-tuned model as a model.

cases.evidence_in_document: Our lawful basis for processing candidate data is the legitimate interests of the employer, recorded in a balancing test annexed to the DPIA. We do not process special categories
cases.rationale: A lawful basis and balancing test are documented and no special categories are used. But using candidates' data to TRAIN the model is a secondary purpose that the employer's legitimate interest may not cover, and reusing hiring-decision data for training raises a purpose-limitation question. Partial pending that analysis. HIGH-VALUE REVIEW: this is a contested GDPR point.

cases.evidence_in_document: We completed a data protection impact assessment in November 2025 covering the training pipeline and the live product.
cases.rationale: Large-scale profiling for employment decisions requires a DPIA; one exists and covers both pipeline and product.

cases.evidence_in_document: The product does not make hiring decisions. Recruiters review the ranked list and decide whom to interview. ... Our privacy notice describes the logic of the scoring in general terms.
cases.rationale: Human review means the decision is not 'solely' automated, so the Article 22(1) prohibition is not triggered. But the duty to give data subjects meaningful information about the logic is only partly met ('general terms'). Partial. REVIEW: could be 'met' if the general-terms description is judged sufficient.

cases.evidence_in_document: Candidates can request access to and deletion of their data ... deletion requests are executed ... within 30 days.
cases.rationale: Access and erasure are handled; rectification and portability are not mentioned. Partial.

cases.evidence_in_document: We hold ISO 27001 certification ... encrypted at rest with AES-256 and in transit with TLS 1.3. Access ... restricted to nine named engineers via SSO with hardware keys.
cases.rationale: Encryption, access control, certification and annual testing evidence Article 32 security appropriate to the risk.

cases.evidence_in_document: a SaaS product
cases.rationale: The Data Act connected-product access duties bind makers of physical connected products. A pure SaaS with no device is out of scope.

cases.evidence_in_document: 'Talentyx Screen', a SaaS product
cases.rationale: The Data Act switching provisions target data processing services in the cloud/edge infrastructure sense (compute, storage, platform). A vertical hiring SaaS is more plausibly outside them. REVIEW: the Data Act definition of 'data processing service' is broad and an aggressive reading could pull a SaaS in, in which case the silence on exit/portability is a gap.

cases.evidence_in_document: We keep a changelog of model versions. ... We maintain an internal model card describing the training data, evaluation results and known limitations.
cases.rationale: The revised Product Liability Directive makes their software a product and their post-market updates a source of liability. They keep the design and test records that mitigate exposure, but there is no evidence of a deliberate liability posture. Partial. Note: this is exposure awareness more than a checkable compliance duty.

cases.evidence_in_document: We maintain an internal model card describing the training data, evaluation results and known limitations.
cases.rationale: The records they keep (model card, changelog, test results) are exactly what a disclosure order under the new PLD would demand, which reduces the risk of an adverse presumption of defect. Partial, since there is no explicit litigation-readiness posture.
